title: Two Eagles, a Vine, and a Cedar
overview: Ezekiel tells a picture story about eagles and plants to explain why Judah's king will fall for breaking his oath to Babylon, then ends with God's promise to plant a new and lasting king.

parts.label: The first eagle (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The great eagle stands for Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and the top of the cedar is Judah's young king Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon in 597 BC. The cedar recalls Jerusalem and David's royal family, and the 'city of traders' is Babylon, a great center of river trade.

parts.label: A low vine is planted (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: The seedling is Zedekiah, a member of the royal family whom Babylon made king in Jehoiachin's place. He could thrive, but only as a low vine leaning on Babylon, not as a tall cedar standing on its own.

parts.label: The vine turns to another eagle (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: The second eagle is Egypt's king, and the vine reaching toward him pictures Zedekiah seeking Egypt's help to break free of Babylon. The east wind stands for Babylon, which lay to the east and would easily uproot him.

parts.label: The riddle explained (vv. 11-15)
parts.note: Ezekiel spells it out plainly: Babylon took Judah's king and leading men away, then made Zedekiah swear loyalty so the weakened kingdom could survive. Zedekiah broke that sworn agreement by sending to Egypt for horses and troops.

parts.label: The oath breaker's fate (vv. 16-21)
parts.note: Because Zedekiah swore his oath in God's name, the text treats breaking it as betraying God, not just Babylon. This came true when Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, Egypt's help failed, and Zedekiah was captured and taken to Babylon, where he died.

parts.label: God plants a new cedar (vv. 22-24)
parts.note: Now God, not a foreign king, takes a tender shoot from David's family tree and plants it on Israel's high mountain, where it becomes a great cedar sheltering every kind of bird. Christians read this shoot as pointing to Jesus, and Jesus' own story of a mustard plant sheltering birds seems to echo it.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the planted shoot in verses 22 to 24 is a direct prediction of Jesus or first a promise to restore David's line after the exile, which Christians later saw fulfilled in him.
think: When a promise made under pressure becomes a burden, what do you think makes it still worth keeping, or worth breaking?
